newsitem.title: FRANCE: Axa-UAP gets nod to sell insurance in China.
newsitem.headline: Axa-UAP gets nod to sell insurance in China.

text.p: French insurance giant Axa-UAP, achieving a long-held ambition, said on Friday it had been given the green light to sell insurance in China.

Peking authorities told President Jacques Chirac during a four-day trade mission to China they would licence Axa-UAP to sell life insurance, making it one of a handful of foreign firms with the coveted authorization, the company said.
The deal was one of a series of agreements, including a $1.5 billion Airbus aircraft order, clinched by Chirac on the high-profile visit during France's parliamentary election campaign.
"It's a medium to long-term project but it is a potentially extraordinary market," an Axa-UAP spokeswoman said.
Axa-UAP, whose chairman Claude Bebear accompanied Chirac on the trip, said procedural hurdles meant it would take at least a year before it was selling policies in China.
The licence will be for Shanghai. Foreign firms currently are only permitted to sell insurance in Shanghai and Guangzhou.

China's insurance market, still in its infancy, was once monopolised by the state-owned People's Insurance Group but it has gradually opened up to local and foreign competition and foreign firms have been jostling to enter.

Axa-UAP, which became the world's second biggest insurer last November when it took over rival UAP, has been working to crack the Chinese market since the early 1990s when China said it would allow foreign insurance firms into the country.
Bebear, who has been aggressively extending Axa's global reach, has forecast the Asian insurance market will eventually be by far the world's largest.
In 1995, Axa bought 51 percent control of Australian life insurer National Mutual, giving it a launching pad for Asia.

To show the seriousness of its wish to be in China, Axa-UAP has begun training Chinese students in western insurance techniques and, last year, it set up a $500 million investment fund targeting primarily China.

The Axa-UAP spokeswoman said the company now had to find a Chinese venture partner to operate in China and it would have to present details of its plans to operate in China to the People's Bank of China to receive final permission.
The Axa spokeswoman said the extent of Natual Mutual's role in China was not finalised. "It seems probable we will work with National Mutual (in China) but we do not know under what conditions."

National Mutual managing director Geoff Tomlinson on Friday said it was good news "that the greater Axa group of companies has secured a licence to operate in China," but cautioned National Mutual investors not to get "too excited".

He said it was not clear whether the National Mutual group would play any role in Axa's success. National Mutual hopes its 69 percent-owned National Mutual Asia subsidiary will own the China business, in a joint venture with local partner China Everbright-IHD Pacific Ltd.
But insurance analysts have expressed doubt Axa-UAP would hand ownership of such a potentially lucrative business to a subsidiary.
Axa-UAP shareholders have only an effective 28 percent interest in National Mutual Asia, and would prefer the Hong Kong company managed the China business for a fee, they suggest.
